claim: PS1 is the catalytic component of γ-secretase.
source: Presenilin 1 (PS1) is the catalytic component of γ-secretase (Wolfe et al., 1999; Esler et al., 2000; Li et al., 2000)
evidence: Supported by three citations to prior research (Wolfe et al., 1999; Esler et al., 2000; Li et al., 2000)

claim: γ-secretase is responsible for the final enzymatic cleavage of APP to generate Aβ.
source: γ-secretase (Wolfe et al., 1999; Esler et al., 2000; Li et al., 2000), which is responsible for the final enzymatic cleavage of amyloid precursor protein (APP) to generate Aβ (De Strooper et al., 1998)
evidence: Supported by citation to De Strooper et al., 1998

claim: Over 180 familial AD mutations have been identified in the PS1 gene.
source: Over 180 familial AD mutations have been identified in the PS1 gene, and the majority of them lead to an increase in the Aβ42/40 ratio (De Strooper, 2007)
evidence: Supported by citation to De Strooper, 2007

claim: The majority of familial AD mutations in PS1 lead to an increase in the Aβ42/40 ratio.
source: Over 180 familial AD mutations have been identified in the PS1 gene, and the majority of them lead to an increase in the Aβ42/40 ratio (De Strooper, 2007)
evidence: Supported by citation to De Strooper, 2007

claim: PS1 knock-in mice carrying familial AD mutations exhibit decreased Aβ40 and Aβ42 levels but increased Aβ42/40 ratio and accelerated Aβ deposition.
source: PS1 knock-in mice carrying familial AD mutations exhibit decreased Aβ40 and Aβ42 levels but increased Aβ42/40 ratio and accelerated Aβ deposition (Xia et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Xia et al., 2015

claim: Up-regulation of the Aβ42/40 ratio rather than the total amount of Aβ has a strong impact on Aβ deposition and AD pathogenesis.
source: This supports the idea that up-regulation of the Aβ42/40 ratio rather than the total amount of Aβ has a strong impact on Aβ deposition and AD pathogenesis.
evidence: Inferred from the PS1 knock-in mouse data cited from Xia et al., 2015

claim: Familial AD mutations in PS1 increase the proximity of PS1 N-terminus to C-terminus or to the large cytoplasmic loop domain, causing the 'closed' pathogenic PS1 conformation.
source: Using Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET)-based imaging techniques we have previously shown that familial AD mutations in PS1 increase the proximity of PS1 N-terminus (NT) to C-terminus (CT) or to the large cytoplasmic loop domain, causing the so called 'closed' pathogenic PS1 conformation (Berezovska et al., 2005; Uemura et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work by the authors (Berezovska et al., 2005; Uemura et al., 2009)

claim: Several nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and PS1/γ-secretase modulators decrease the Aβ42/40 ratio.
source: On the other hand, several nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and PS1/γ-secretase modulators, which are known to decrease the Aβ42/40 ratio (Weggen et al., 2001; Page et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citations to Weggen et al., 2001 and Page et al., 2008

claim: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and PS1/γ-secretase modulators drive PS1 into the 'open' conformation.
source: several nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and PS1/γ-secretase modulators, which are known to decrease the Aβ42/40 ratio (Weggen et al., 2001; Page et al., 2008), drive PS1 into the 'open' conformation (Lleó et al., 2004; Uemura et al., 2009; Ohki et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to Lleó et al., 2004; Uemura et al., 2009; Ohki et al., 2011

claim: PS1 conformational changes are tightly linked to changes of the Aβ42/40 ratio.
source: These reports indicate that PS1 conformational changes are tightly linked to changes of the Aβ42/40 ratio
evidence: Inferred from the cited studies showing that mutations causing closed conformation increase Aβ42/40 ratio and modulators causing open conformation decrease it

claim: Modulation of the pathogenic 'closed' PS1 conformation is a potential target for AD treatment.
source: suggesting that modulation of the pathogenic 'closed' PS1 conformation is a potential target for AD treatment
evidence: Speculative conclusion based on the link between PS1 conformation and Aβ42/40 ratio

claim: Aβ deposition is observed in brain regions exhibiting a high basal rate of neuronal activity in humans.
source: Notably, Aβ deposition is observed in brain regions exhibiting a high basal rate of neuronal activity in humans (Sperling et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citation to Sperling et al., 2009

claim: Aβ causes Ca2+ elevation.
source: The idea that Aβ causes Ca2+ elevation is supported by several studies (Kuchibhotla et al., 2008; Lopez et al., 2008; Busche et al., 2012; Higuchi et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations (Kuchibhotla et al., 2008; Lopez et al., 2008; Busche et al., 2012; Higuchi et al., 2012)

claim: Acute stimulation of the entorhinal cortex using an optogenetic approach increases the Aβ42 level specifically in the projection area of the perforant pathway.
source: For example, acute stimulation of the entorhinal cortex using an optogenetic approach increases the Aβ42 level specifically in the projection area of the perforant pathway (Yamamoto et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Yamamoto et al., 2015

claim: KCl-induced depolarization causes sustained release of Aβ42 from AD mouse model synaptoneurosomes.
source: KCl-induced depolarization causes sustained release of Aβ42 from AD mouse model synaptoneurosomes (Kim et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim et al., 2010

claim: KCl-triggered Ca2+ influx elevates intracellular Aβ42/40 ratio in primary neurons.
source: KCl-triggered Ca2+ influx elevates intracellular Aβ42/40 ratio in primary neurons (Pierrot et al., 2004)
evidence: Supported by citation to Pierrot et al., 2004

claim: Increases in Ca2+ levels induce the PS1 pathogenic 'closed' conformation in primary neurons, followed by an increase in the Aβ42/40 ratio.
source: We recently reported that increases in Ca2+ levels induce the PS1 pathogenic 'closed' conformation in primary neurons, followed by an increase in the Aβ42/40 ratio (Kuzuya et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work by the authors (Kuzuya et al., 2016)

claim: PS1 is found in the 'closed' conformation in sporadic AD brain.
source: Furthermore, PS1 is found in the 'closed' conformation in sporadic AD brain, and this pathogenic PS1 conformational shift correlates with the proximity to deposited Aβ (Wahlster et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Wahlster et al., 2013

claim: The pathogenic PS1 conformational shift correlates with the proximity to deposited Aβ in sporadic AD brain.
source: Furthermore, PS1 is found in the 'closed' conformation in sporadic AD brain, and this pathogenic PS1 conformational shift correlates with the proximity to deposited Aβ (Wahlster et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Wahlster et al., 2013

claim: Fifteen phosphorylation sites have been identified in PS1.
source: In PS1, fifteen phosphorylation sites have been identified (Kirschenbaum et al., 2001; Lau et al., 2002; Fluhrer et al., 2004; Kuo et al., 2008; Ryu et al., 2010; Matz et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations (Kirschenbaum et al., 2001; Lau et al., 2002; Fluhrer et al., 2004; Kuo et al., 2008; Ryu et al., 2010; Matz et al., 2015)

claim: Phosphorylation of some PS1 sites affects the stability of PS1/γ-secretase.
source: Although the phosphorylation of some of these sites affects the stability of PS1/γ-secretase (Lau et al., 2002; Kuo et al., 2008; Ryu et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to Lau et al., 2002; Kuo et al., 2008; Ryu et al., 2010

claim: KCl treatment significantly increased the proximity between fluorescently labeled PS1 N-terminus and PS1 C-terminus in primary neurons.
source: We show that treatment with KCl significantly increased the proximity between fluorescently labeled PS1 N-terminus (NT) and PS1 C-terminus (CT) (increased red pixels mean higher FRET efficiency, Figure 1A)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A using FLIM analysis

claim: KCl treatment triggers the 'closed' conformation of endogenous PS1.
source: indicating that KCl treatment triggers the 'closed' conformation of endogenous PS1
evidence: Inferred from the FRET data showing increased proximity between PS1 NT and CT

claim: KCl treatment significantly increased the level of PS1 phosphorylation at its serine residues.
source: We found that KCl treatment significantly increased the level of PS1 phosphorylation at its serine residues (Figure 1B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B using immunoprecipitation/Western blot analysis

claim: Glutamate treatment increases PS1 phosphorylation.
source: We have confirmed this finding using another stimulant, glutamate (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Ca2+ influx leads to PS1 phosphorylation.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that Ca2+ influx leads to PS1 phosphorylation.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing KCl and glutamate (both causing Ca2+ influx) increase PS1 phosphorylation

claim: A23187 significantly increased the FRET efficiency between fluorescently labeled NT and CT of WT PS1.
source: A23187 significantly increased the FRET efficiency between fluorescently labeled NT and CT of WT PS1 (Table 1)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Table 1

claim: WT PS1 adopts the 'closed' conformation following treatment with the Ca2+ ionophore A23187.
source: This indicates that WT PS1 adopts the 'closed' conformation following the treatment with the Ca2+ ionophore.
evidence: Inferred from FRET data showing increased FRET efficiency after A23187 treatment

claim: A23187 did not change the FRET efficiencies in T74A, S310A, S313A, S310A/S313A, S365A, S366A, S367A, S365A/S367A and S366A/S367A PS1 transfected cells.
source: On the other hand, A23187 did not change the FRET efficiencies in T74A, S310A, S313A, S310A/S313A, S365A, S366A, S367A, S365A/S367A and S366A/S367A PS1 transfected cells, suggesting that conformation of these PS1 mutants was resistant to Ca2+ ionophore treatment (Table 1)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Table 1

claim: The conformation of phosphorylation-inhibited PS1 mutants (T74A, S310A, S313A, S310A/S313A, S365A, S366A, S367A, S365A/S367A and S366A/S367A) was resistant to Ca2+ ionophore treatment.
source: On the other hand, A23187 did not change the FRET efficiencies in T74A, S310A, S313A, S310A/S313A, S365A, S366A, S367A, S365A/S367A and S366A/S367A PS1 transfected cells, suggesting that conformation of these PS1 mutants was resistant to Ca2+ ionophore treatment (Table 1)
evidence: Inferred from FRET data showing no change in FRET efficiency after A23187 treatment

claim: The A23187-resistant phosphorylation sites on PS1 can be divided into three sub-membrane domains: domain 1 (T74) on NT of PS1, domain 2 (S310, S313) and domain 3 (S365, S366, S367) within the large hydrophilic loop.
source: The A23187-resistant phosphorylation sites on PS1 could be divided into three sub-membrane domains: domain 1 (T74) on NT of PS1, domain 2 (S310, S313) and domain 3 (S365, S366, S367) within the large hydrophilic loop (Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Based on analysis of the phosphorylation-inhibited mutants that resist A23187-induced conformational change

claim: There was no statistical difference between the FRET efficiencies of WT PS1 and phosphorylation-inhibited PS1 mutants in vehicle-treated cells.
source: There was no statistical difference between the FRET efficiencies of WT PS1 and phosphorylation-inhibited PS1 mutants in vehicle-treated cells (Table 1)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Table 1

claim: The conformation of the phosphorylation-inhibited PS1 mutants is not different from that of WT PS1 in basal conditions.
source: indicating that the conformation of the phosphorylation-inhibited PS1 mutants is not different from that of WT PS1 in basal conditions
evidence: Inferred from FRET data showing no statistical difference in basal conditions

claim: Phosphorylation of domain 1 (T74), domain 2 (S310, S313) and domain 3 (S365, S366, S367) is necessary for the Ca2+ dependent PS1 pathogenic conformational shift.
source: Collectively, these results demonstrate that phosphorylation of the three domains is necessary for the Ca2+ dependent PS1 pathogenic conformational shift.
evidence: Inferred from data showing phosphorylation-inhibited mutants in these domains resist Ca2+-induced conformational change

claim: The FRET efficiency of the domain 3 phosphorylation-mimicking G-PS1-R isoform was significantly higher than that of WT G-PS1-R.
source: However, the FRET efficiency of the domain 3 phosphorylation-mimicking G-PS1-R isoform was significantly higher than that of WT G-PS1-R, indicating that this mutant forces PS1 into the 'closed' conformation (Figure 2A)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: The domain 3 phosphorylation-mimicking G-PS1-R mutant forces PS1 into the 'closed' conformation.
source: However, the FRET efficiency of the domain 3 phosphorylation-mimicking G-PS1-R isoform was significantly higher than that of WT G-PS1-R, indicating that this mutant forces PS1 into the 'closed' conformation (Figure 2A)
evidence: Inferred from FRET data showing increased FRET efficiency

claim: Domains 1 + 3 G-PS1-R, domains 2 + 3 G-PS1-R and domains 1 + 2 + 3 G-PS1-R adopted the 'closed' conformation.
source: Domains 1 + 3 G-PS1-R, domains 2 + 3 G-PS1-R and domains 1 + 2 + 3 G-PS1-R also adopted the 'closed' conformation (Figure 2A)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Phosphorylation of domain 3 is the critical mechanism leading to the PS1/γ-secretase pathogenic 'closed' conformation.
source: Collectively, these results strongly suggest that phosphorylation of domain 3 is the critical mechanism leading to the PS1/γ-secretase pathogenic 'closed' conformation.
evidence: Inferred from data showing domain 3 phosphorylation-mimicking mutants adopt closed conformation while domain 1 or 2 alone do not

claim: The FRET efficiency of S367D G-PS1-R was significantly higher than that of WT G-PS1-R.
source: The spectral FRET analysis revealed significantly higher FRET efficiency in S367D G-PS1-R but not in S365D G-PS1-R or S366D G-PS1-R, as compared to WT G-PS1-R (Figure 2B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Phosphorylation of PS1 at serine 367 is responsible for the PS1 'closed' conformational change.
source: This indicates that phosphorylation of PS1 at serine 367 is responsible for the PS1 'closed' conformational change.
evidence: Inferred from FRET data showing only S367D mutant has increased FRET efficiency

claim: Only the PKA inhibitor (KT5720) specifically rescued the Ca2+-triggered 'closed' PS1 conformation, whereas JNK, PKC and GSK3β inhibitors did not.
source: The spectral FRET assay revealed that only the PKA inhibitor (KT5720) specifically rescued the Ca2+-triggered 'closed' PS1 conformation, whereas JNK, PKC and GSK3β inhibitors did not (Figure 3A)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: PKA activity is involved in the Ca2+-triggered PS1 pathogenic conformational change.
source: To address this, WT G-PS1-R expressing 7 W cells were incubated with inhibitors of several kinases prior to A23187 treatment. The spectral FRET assay revealed that only the PKA inhibitor (KT5720) specifically rescued the Ca2+-triggered 'closed' PS1 conformation
evidence: Inferred from data showing PKA inhibitor prevents Ca2+-induced conformational change

claim: The proximity between the fluorescently labelled PS1 NT and CT was comparable between vehicle and KCl-treated neurons in the presence of H-89 or KT5720.
source: We found that the proximity between the fluorescently labelled PS1 NT and CT was comparable between vehicle and KCl-treated neurons in the presence of H-89 or KT5720 (Figure 3B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: The FRET efficiency of forskolin or 8-Bromo-cAMP treated neurons was significantly higher than that of vehicle-treated neurons.
source: On the other hand, the FRET efficiency of forskolin or 8-Bromo-cAMP treated neurons was significantly higher than that of vehicle-treated neurons (Figure 3B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: There was no additive effect with KCl and PKA activators on PS1 conformation.
source: Of note, there was no additive effect with KCl and PKA activators (Figure 3B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: EGTA decreased the FRET efficiency between PS1 NT and CT, indicating that PS1 adopted an 'open' conformation.
source: As expected, EGTA decreased the FRET efficiency between PS1 NT and CT, indicating that PS1 adopted an 'open' conformation (Figure 3C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: EGTA had no effect on PS1 conformation in the presence of PKA activators.
source: On the other hand, EGTA had no effect on PS1 conformation in the presence of PKA activators (Figure 3C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: PKA activation is an event down-stream of the Ca2+ influx.
source: indicating that PKA activation is an event down-stream of the Ca2+ influx
evidence: Inferred from data showing EGTA cannot reverse PKA activator effects

claim: PKA activation by forskolin caused the PS1 'closed' conformation in WT G-PS1-R expressing cells.
source: Whereas PKA activation by forskolin caused the PS1 'closed' conformation in WT G-PS1-R expressing cells, it did not affect the conformation of domain 1, domain 2, or domain 3 phosphorylation-inhibited mutants (Figure 3D)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Forskolin did not affect the conformation of domain 1, domain 2, or domain 3 phosphorylation-inhibited mutants.
source: Whereas PKA activation by forskolin caused the PS1 'closed' conformation in WT G-PS1-R expressing cells, it did not affect the conformation of domain 1, domain 2, or domain 3 phosphorylation-inhibited mutants (Figure 3D)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Blocking phosphorylation of either domain 1, 2, or 3 precludes PS1 from adopting the 'closed' conformation via PKA activation.
source: This indicates that blocking phosphorylation of either one of these domains precludes PS1 from adopting the 'closed' conformation via PKA activation.

claim: The FRET efficiency of domains 1 + 2 phosphorylation-mimicking G-PS1-R was significantly increased upon A23187, forskolin or 8-Bromo-cAMP treatments.
source: Similar to WT G-PS1-R expressing cells, the FRET efficiency of domains 1 + 2 phosphorylation-mimicking G-PS1-R was significantly increased upon A23187, forskolin or 8-Bromo-cAMP treatments (Figure 3E)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E

claim: PKA is involved in the phosphorylation of S365-S366-S367 residues.
source: This indicates that PKA is involved in the phosphorylation of S365-S366-S367 residues.
evidence: Inferred from data showing PKA activators can induce closed conformation even when domains 1+2 are already phosphorylated

claim: Treatment with KT5720 abolished the KCl-induced elevation of the Aβ42/40 ratio.

evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F using ELISA

claim: Phosphorylation of domain 1 or 2 is not sufficient for the PS1 conformational change, but is required for PKA-mediated phosphorylation of domain 3, leading to the pathogenic conformational change in PS1/γ-secretase.
source: Collectively, these data demonstrate that phosphorylation of domain 1 or 2 is not sufficient for the PS1 conformational change, but is required for PKA-mediated phosphorylation of domain 3, leading to the pathogenic conformational change in PS1/γ-secretase.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments showing domain 1+2 phosphorylation alone doesn't cause closed conformation but is needed for domain 3 phosphorylation

claim: GFP emission was the strongest in the 875–900 nm wavelength range.
source: First, we found that GFP emission was the strongest in the 875–900 nm wavelength range, whereas RFP emission significantly decreased at >800 nm excitation, with barely detectable RFP signal at 900 nm in 7 W cells expressing G-PS1-R (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: RFP emission significantly decreased at >800 nm excitation, with barely detectable RFP signal at 900 nm in 7 W cells expressing G-PS1-R.
source: First, we found that GFP emission was the strongest in the 875–900 nm wavelength range, whereas RFP emission significantly decreased at >800 nm excitation, with barely detectable RFP signal at 900 nm in 7 W cells expressing G-PS1-R (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: The emission intensity of RFP at 900 nm excitation is caused neither by GFP fluorescence bleed-through, nor by direct RFP excitation.

claim: The R/G ratio was significantly higher in G-PS1-R expressing neurons than that in G-PS1 (donor only).

evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Topical KCl application significantly increased intracellular Ca2+ levels in the somatosensory cortex neurons.

evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: The actual concentration of Ca2+ in cell bodies was increased from ~58 nM at the basal condition up to ~2793 nM immediately after the applied KCl reached the imaging site.

evidence: Supported by experimental data using YC3.6 Ca2+ imaging

claim: Ca2+ remained at ~166 nM during the 2 min of imaging (mean = ~649 nM) after KCl application.
source: It remained at ~166 nM during the 2 min of imaging (mean = ~649 nM).
evidence: Supported by experimental data using YC3.6 Ca2+ imaging

claim: The R/G ratio was significantly enhanced by the KCl application in WT G-PS1-R expressing neurons.
source: Consistently, the R/G ratio was significantly enhanced by the KCl application (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 3)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 3

claim: Elevated Ca2+ induces the pathogenic PS1 conformation in vivo.
source: indicating that elevated Ca2+ induces the pathogenic PS1 conformation in vivo

claim: No change in the R/G ratio was detected in neurons expressing S365A/S366A/S367A G-PS1-R mutant after KCl application.

claim: Increased intracellular Ca2+ triggers the 'closed' conformation of PS1 via domain 3 phosphorylation in vivo.

claim: PKA activation by 8-Bromo-cAMP led to the 'closed' conformation of endogenous PS1 in mouse brain.

claim: PKA inhibition by KT5720 could prevent the 8-Bromo-cAMP-triggered 'closed' conformation of PS1 in mouse brain.

claim: The average PS1 phosphorylation at S310 is significantly increased in AD brains as compared to non-demented control brains.

claim: Neither age nor PMI significantly affected the level of PS1 phosphorylation in both control and AD cases.

claim: Ca2+/PKA-mediated PS1 phosphorylation at domain 1 (T74), domain 2 (S310, S313) and domain 3 (S365, S366, S367) is responsible for the PS1/γ-secretase pathogenic conformational change in vitro and in vivo.
source: Our current study addresses these questions and demonstrates that Ca2+/PKA-mediated PS1 phosphorylation at domain 1 (T74), domain 2 (S310, S313) and domain 3 (S365, S366, S367) is responsible for the PS1/γ-secretase pathogenic conformational change in vitro and in vivo.

claim: The high level of serines and threonines in the PS1 N-terminus and in the large hydrophilic loop region suggests that the enzymatic function of PS1 can be modulated by its 'phosphorylated' and 'dephosphorylated' states.
source: The high level of serines and threonines in the PS1 N-terminus and in the large hydrophilic loop region suggests that the enzymatic function of PS1 can be modulated by its 'phosphorylated' and 'dephosphorylated' states.

claim: PS1 phosphorylation at several residues enhances stability of the PS1 CT fragment that is necessary for γ-secretase activity.

claim: Matz and colleagues have identified eleven new phosphorylation sites in PS1.

claim: Phosphorylation-inhibited mutations of eleven PS1 sites affect neither activity of the PS1/γ-secretase nor Aβ production.

claim: The conformation of the phosphorylation-inhibited PS1 mutants at T74, S310, S313, S365, S366 and S367 is not different from that of the WT PS1 in basal conditions.
source: We found that the conformation of the phosphorylation-inhibited PS1 mutants at these residues is not different from that of the WT PS1.

claim: The conformation of the phosphorylation-inhibiting mutants and WT PS1 is very different in the Ca2+ influx-stimulated condition.

claim: Phosphorylation of PS1 at T74, S310, S313, S365, S366 and S367 as a result of the Ca2+ influx/PKA activation underlies its conformational change.

claim: Phosphorylation of domain 1 and domain 2, though necessary, is not sufficient for the structural change of PS1.

claim: Domain 3, specifically S367, is critical for PS1 achieving the 'closed' conformation.

claim: PKA first phosphorylates PS1 at domain 2, which leads to spatial rearrangements around domain 1, and allows its phosphorylation.

claim: Phosphorylation of domain 1 subsequently changes the local conformation around domain 3, enabling its phosphorylation by PKA.
source: This subsequently changes the local conformation around domain 3, enabling its phosphorylation by PKA.

claim: Phosphorylation of S365-S366-S367, with S367 being most crucial, drives the pathogenic conformational alteration of the PS1/γ-secretase.

claim: Local spatial rearrangement around domain three is a key step for PKA-induced domain three phosphorylation.

evidence: Proposed model based on experimental data and inference

claim: Phosphorylation of domain 1 and domain 2 is necessary for local spatial rearrangement around domain 3.
source: We propose that local spatial rearrangement around domain three is a key step for PKA-induced domain three phosphorylation, and phosphorylation of domain 1 and domain 2 is necessary for this to occur.
evidence: Proposed model based on experimental data and inference

claim: PKA is able to phosphorylate only S310 within domain 2 in recombinant PS1 hydrophilic loop (263–407) peptide in vitro.
source: This model is consistent with the finding that PKA is able to phosphorylate only S310 within domain 2 in recombinant PS1 hydrophilic loop (263–407) peptide in vitro (Fluhrer et al., 2004)
evidence: Supported by citation to Fluhrer et al., 2004

claim: Lack of domain 1 in recombinant PS1 fragment does not allow change in the local conformation around domain 3, explaining why S365-S366-S367 are not phosphorylated by PKA in this recombinant PS1.
source: We reason that lack of domain 1 in this recombinant PS1 fragment does not allow change in the local conformation around domain 3, explaining why S365-S366-S367 are not phosphorylated by PKA in this recombinant PS1.
evidence: Inferred explanation for why PKA only phosphorylates S310 in recombinant PS1 fragment

claim: 350–373 residues of PS1 containing domain 3 are subject to major movements.
source: Moreover, a recent structural simulation study has demonstrated that 350–373 residues of PS1 containing domain 3, are subject to major movements (Somavarapu and Kepp, 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to Somavarapu and Kepp, 2016

claim: Naturally occurring domain 1 and domain 2 phosphorylation events may trigger local spatial rearrangements around the 350–373 residues of PS1.
source: It is highly likely that naturally occurring domain 1 and domain 2 phosphorylation events may trigger these local spatial rearrangements around the 350–373 residues of PS1.
evidence: Speculative inference based on structural simulation data and phosphorylation data

claim: Domain 1 or domain 3 phosphorylation-inhibited mutant PS1 were still able to get phosphorylated by PKA at domain 2.
source: We confirmed that domain 1 or domain 3 phosphorylation-inhibited mutant PS1 were still able to get phosphorylated by PKA at domain 2 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B

claim: Domain 2 is the first step of the phosphorylation.
source: suggesting that domain 2 is the first step of the phosphorylation
evidence: Inferred from data showing domain 2 can be phosphorylated even when domain 1 or 3 are blocked

claim: Except for domain 2, there are no known PKA substrate consensus sequences around domain 1 or domain 3 of PS1.
source: Consistently, except for domain 2, there are no known PKA substrate consensus sequences (Ubersax and Ferrell, 2007) around domain 1 or domain 3 of PS1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: Based on sequence analysis and established knowledge of PKA consensus sequences

claim: Topical KCl application significantly increased intracellular Ca2+ (mean = ~649 nM, ranging from 166 nM to 2793 nM) in WT mice brains.
source: Topical KCl application significantly increased intracellular Ca2+ (mean = ~649 nM, ranging from 166 nM to 2793 nM) in WT mice brains
evidence: Supported by experimental data using YC3.6 Ca2+ imaging in vivo

claim: The concentration of Ca2+ observed after KCl application is consistent with that observed in AD mouse models displaying Ca2+ overload in vivo (mean = ~499 nM, ranging from 162 nM to 1535 nM).
source: a concentration of Ca2+ consistent with that observed in AD mouse models displaying Ca2+ overload in vivo (mean = ~499 nM, ranging from 162 nM to 1535 nM) (Kuchibhotla et al., 2008)
evidence: Comparison with data from Kuchibhotla et al., 2008

claim: Ca2+ influx induces the pathogenic 'closed' PS1 conformation in vivo via PS1 S365/S366/S367 phosphorylation.
source: We verified that Ca2+ influx induces the pathogenic 'closed' PS1 conformation in vivo via PS1 S365/S366/S367 phosphorylation.
evidence: Supported by in vivo experimental data showing KCl induces closed conformation in WT but not in S365A/S366A/S367A mutant

claim: PKA-mediated PS1 phosphorylation is involved in the conformational change of the endogenous PS1.
source: To ensure that PKA-mediated phosphorylation is involved in the conformational change of the endogenous PS1, 8-Bromo-cAMP and vehicle control were injected into the somatosensory cortex of mice
evidence: Supported by ex vivo experimental data showing PKA activation induces closed conformation

claim: A wide distribution of the phosphorylated PS1 levels observed in AD cases did not correlate with either age or PMI.
source: Of note, a wide distribution of the phosphorylated PS1 levels observed in AD cases did not correlate with either age or PMI.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2

claim: Once AD pathology triggers Ca2+ overload, domains 1, 2 and 3 of PS1 can be hyper-phosphorylated by PKA.
source: We propose a positive feed-forward mechanism for the pathogenesis of AD (Figure 6): once AD pathology, i.e. Aβ oligomers or deposited Aβ, triggers Ca2+ overload, domains 1, 2 and 3 of PS1 can be hyper-phosphorylated by PKA.
evidence: Proposed model based on experimental findings

claim: PS1 hyper-phosphorylation induces the pathogenic 'closed' PS1 conformation, and leads to subsequent elevation of the Aβ42/40 ratio, followed by accelerated Aβ oligomerization or deposition.
source: This induces the pathogenic 'closed' PS1 conformation, and leads to subsequent elevation of the Aβ42/40 ratio, followed by accelerated Aβ oligomerization or deposition.
evidence: Proposed model based on experimental findings

claim: Higher Aβ42/40 ratio leads to the pathogenic conformation of PS1/γ-secretase.
source: In line with these findings, we have previously reported that PS1 shows a 'closed' conformation around Aβ plaques in the sporadic AD brain (Wahlster et al., 2013), and that higher Aβ42/40 ratio leads to the pathogenic conformation of PS1/γ-secretase (Zoltowska et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work by the authors (Wahlster et al., 2013; Zoltowska et al., 2016)

claim: Selective inhibition of PS1 phosphorylation at the domain 1, 2 and/or 3 may present a novel opportunity for therapeutics for AD.
source: It is conceivable that selective inhibition of PS1 phosphorylation at the domain 1, 2 and/or 3 may present a novel opportunity for therapeutics for AD.
evidence: Speculative conclusion based on the findings

claim: Phosphorylation-inhibited PS1 mutations on domain 1, 2, and 3 sites do not affect assembly, maturation, or activity of the PS1/γ-secretase.
source: Since phosphorylation-inhibited PS1 mutations on these sites do not affect assembly, maturation, or activity of the PS1/γ-secretase (Matz et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Matz et al., 2015

claim: Inhibition of PS1 phosphorylation at domain 1, 2, and 3 residues would affect neither the cleavage of Notch nor other γ-secretase substrates.
source: inhibition of these PS1 phosphorylation residues would affect neither the cleavage of Notch nor other γ-secretase substrates
evidence: Inferred from data showing phosphorylation-inhibited mutants don't affect γ-secretase activity

claim: Inhibition of PKA activity may not be a suitable approach to prevent PS1 phosphorylation, due to multiple PKA substrates and potential off target effects in the brain and in the periphery.
source: On the other hand, inhibition of PKA activity may not be a suitable approach to prevent PS1 phosphorylation, due to multiple PKA substrates and potential off target effects in the brain and in the periphery.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about PKA having multiple substrates

claim: Activity-driven and Protein Kinase A-mediated PS1 phosphorylation at three domains (domain 1: T74, domain 2: S310 and S313, domain 3: S365, S366, and S367), with S367 being critical, is responsible for the PS1 pathogenic 'closed' conformation.
source: Here, comprehensive analysis using FRET-based imaging reveals that activity-driven and Protein Kinase A-mediated PS1 phosphorylation at three domains (domain 1: T74, domain 2: S310 and S313, domain 3: S365, S366, and S367), with S367 being critical, is responsible for the PS1 pathogenic 'closed' conformation, and resulting increase in the Aβ42/40 ratio.
evidence: Supported by comprehensive experimental data throughout the manuscript

claim: PS1 phosphorylation at three domains results in an increase in the Aβ42/40 ratio.
source: Here, comprehensive analysis using FRET-based imaging reveals that activity-driven and Protein Kinase A-mediated PS1 phosphorylation at three domains (domain 1: T74, domain 2: S310 and S313, domain 3: S365, S366, and S367), with S367 being critical, is responsible for the PS1 pathogenic 'closed' conformation, and resulting increase in the Aβ42/40 ratio.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing PKA inhibitor prevents KCl-induced increase in Aβ42/40 ratio

claim: Novel imaging assays for monitoring PS1 conformation in vivo have been established.
source: Moreover, we have established novel imaging assays for monitoring PS1 conformation in vivo
evidence: Supported by development and validation of in vivo spectral FRET assay

claim: PS1 phosphorylation induces the pathogenic conformational shift in the living mouse brain.
source: and report that PS1 phosphorylation induces the pathogenic conformational shift in the living mouse brain
evidence: Supported by in vivo experimental data

claim: PS1 phosphorylation sites at domains 1, 2, and 3 represent potential new targets for AD treatment.
source: These phosphorylation sites represent potential new targets for AD treatment.
evidence: Speculative conclusion based on the findings

claim: Co-expression of the G324D PKA mutant together with G-PS1-R prevents both Ca2+-triggered PS1 phosphorylation at S310 and the 'closed' PS1 conformation.
source: We found that co-expression of the G324D PKA mutant together with G-PS1-R prevents both Ca2+-triggered PS1 phosphorylation at S310 and the 'closed' PS1 conformation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D

claim: CREB is a well known PKA-specific substrate.
source: The cAMP response element binding protein (CREB), a well known PKA-specific substrate (Gonzalez and Montminy, 1989)
evidence: Supported by citation to Gonzalez and Montminy, 1989
